Operating the system over time
Getting the agent to production is one milestone. Keeping it reliable, cost-efficient, and
accurate as usage grows and documentation evolves is the ongoing work. Three areas deserve
explicit attention once the system is live.
Scaling the agentic system
The vehicle-support-assistant as idx_61b547acidx_54ae04a4 configured in this chapter handles one conversation at a time
in a single region. As call center usage grows, a few decisions become necessary:
Throughput and quota: GPT-4.1 deployments in Microsoft Foundry are subject to
tokens-per-minute (TPM) quotas. If the agent starts handling concurrent calls at
scale, you will hit rate limits before you hit infrastructure limits. Monitor your TPM
consumption in Application Insights and request quota increases proactively — not
after users start seeing delays.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 256
chunks.content:
Chapter 10 256
Multi-region deployment: If your call center operates across geographies, a single
Azure region introduces latency and availability risk. Microsoft Foundry supports
deploying the same agent configuration to multiple regions. Each region gets its own
model deployment, but both can point to the same knowledge base if it is hosted in a
globally accessible resource. Alternatively, replicate the knowledge base per region for
lower retrieval latency in high-volume scenarios.
Session management at scale: The agent as configured is stateless between
conversations — each call starts fresh. For a call center where an agent might handle a
follow-up call from the same customer, consider passing relevant session context in the
system prompt dynamically. This avoids the agent asking for information the customer
already provided in a previous interaction.
Cost optimization
Running a idx_46206921idx_9acaa41d production AI system has real cost implications across three dimensions: inference,
retrieval, and monitoring.
Inference cost is driven by token consumption per conversation — the system prompt,
the retrieved document chunks, and the response all count. The system prompt in this
chapter is approximately 300 tokens. Every retrieval adds chunks on top of that. A long
conversation with multiple retrievals can easily reach 4,000–6,000 tokens per turn. To
control this: keep the system prompt as concise as possible without sacrificing
precision, limit the number of chunks returned per retrieval query (Foundry IQ allows
configuring retrieval depth), and set a maximum conversation turn limit for the agent.
Retrieval idx_2e0c36ebidx_a40fd0c6 cost scales with the size of your knowledge base and the frequency of re-
indexing. Re-indexing every document every night when only one file changed is
wasteful. Configure incremental indexing — only documents that have been updated
since the last run should be re-processed. This is especially relevant when the
knowledge base grows beyond a few dozen files.
Evaluation cost is easy to overlook. Each evaluation run consumes tokens from both
the target model and the judge model. A full evaluation run against 80 prompts with
five metrics can cost as much as several hundred API calls. Run full evaluations on
release events; use lighter targeted runs (20–30 prompts) for routine change
validation.
A practical starting point would be to instrument your Application Insights dashboard to track
average tokens per conversation and cost per session. This gives you a baseline from day one
and makes cost anomalies visible before they accumulate.

Managing the knowledge base over time
The knowledge base is not a idx_c6856d89idx_bf869322 static asset. Warranty policies get updated, recall notices expire,

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 256
chunks.content:
maintenance schedules change with new vehicle models, and dealer SOPs evolve with
operational changes. An agent grounded in outdated documents is worse than no agent—it
answers confidently with wrong information.
A sustainable knowledge base management practice covers three habits:
Document versioning and ownership: Every document in the knowledge base should
have a designated owner — the person or team responsible for keeping it current.
When a policy changes, the owner updates the file and triggers a re-index. Without
ownership, documents go stale with no one noticing.
Scheduled review cadence: Set a recurring calendar reminder — monthly for high-
volatility documents like recall notices, quarterly for stable documents like standard
warranty terms — to verify that indexed content still matches the approved source. A
simple spot-check: run five test queries against topics covered by each document and
confirm the responses still cite the current version.
Retirement and replacement: When a document is superseded, remove it from the
knowledge base before adding the replacement. Leaving both versions indexed creates
retrieval ambiguity — the agent may cite the outdated version for some queries and
the new version for others, producing inconsistent answers. The correct sequence is:
remove old document → confirm removal → add new document → verify indexing →
run targeted evaluation before re-enabling the affected query categories.
These idx_aee1d8fcidx_18f1dc6b three areas (scaling, cost, and knowledge base maintenance) are not afterthoughts. They
are what separate a successful pilot from a system that the call center team actually trusts and
relies on six months after launch.
Summary
In this chapter, you scoped a realistic vehicle post-sell support call center scenario and
translated it into a Foundry-first build plan with clear boundaries, success criteria, and safe
defaults. You then created a project in the new Microsoft Foundry portal, connected your
knowledge sources, built an agent with grounded instructions, and assembled workflows that
match how real call centers operate—especially when escalation and human review matter.
You also walked through the practical portal steps to deploy and operate the solution:
configuring actions, testing with representative call samples, and setting up monitoring so you
can see what's happening in production instead of guessing.

Creating Custom Copilots with
Microsoft Fabric
In this chapter, we will build a customer-facing banking assistant that helps users get answers
about their bank accounts, products, and services. The agent runs inside Microsoft Foundry
and connects to a Microsoft Fabric instance that holds structured data about customer
financial information — account balances, active products, transaction history, and service
status. Like in the previous chapters, everything is configured through the new Microsoft
Foundry portal, with Python only where the portal cannot cover a specific step. By the end of
this chapter, you will have a fully deployed agent that retrieves live financial data safely,
enforces strict identity and data minimization rules, and operates within the compliance
boundaries that a regulated banking environment requires.
What makes this use case different from others is the nature of the data involved. Financial
information is among the most sensitive data a customer can share — and among the most
regulated. That means every design decision in this chapter, from how the agent asks for an
identifier to how it formats a balance response, is shaped by the need to minimize data
exposure, prevent unauthorized access, and maintain a clear and auditable boundary between
what the agent can do and what it cannot.
The chapter follows the same structure as the previous ones. We start by defining the scope
and assumptions, then configure the Microsoft Foundry workspace, connect Microsoft Fabric
as the data source, build and configure the agent, add guardrails and compliance controls, run
evaluations against a banking-specific test dataset, and finally deploy and monitor the agent in
production.
We will cover the topics under the following main headings:

Technical requirements
For this chapter, you will need the following in place before starting:
An active Azure subscription with Contributor rights on a resource group
A Microsoft Fabric capacity (F2 or higher) with at least one published Fabric Data
Agent covering customer banking data. Row-level security and column-level security
are configured on the Fabric datasets before connecting them to the agent
GPT-4.1 quota is available in the target Azure region
Scope and assumptions
This section defines the exact boundaries of what the banking assistant will and will not do.
Working through it carefully before touching any portal configuration avoids rework later — a
guardrail is much harder to add after the agent is live than before it is built. The following
subsections cover in-scope scenarios, out-of-scope restrictions, identity and authentication
assumptions, data exposure principles, the architecture overview, and the success criteria that
must be met before deployment.
In-scope scenarios
The agent handles customer idx_6848dceeidx_fe69d139 questions about their own banking products and services. Every
in-scope question requires the agent to retrieve data from Microsoft Fabric — the agent does
not answer personal financial questions from idx_fa6012d1idx_4802904f memory.
The following scenarios are the ones the agent is designed and tested to handle. Each one
requires a live query to Microsoft Fabric — the agent does not answer personal financial
questions from memory or training data:
"What is my current account balance?"
"What products do I have with this bank?"
"Show me my last five transactions."

"Is my credit card still active?"
"What is the interest rate on my loan?"
The agent may also receive hybrid questions where one part is general and the other is
personal: "How does the cashback program work, and how much cashback have I earned this
month?" In such a case, the agent answers the general part from its instructions and calls the
Microsoft Fabric connector for the personal data component in the same response.
Out-of-scope scenarios
The agent is strictly scoped to idx_c804f3f4idx_58f7d7f9 read-only account information retrieval. The following
categories are explicitly out of scope and must be blocked or escalated rather than handled:
Executing transactions: The agent is strictly read-only. It cannot initiate transfers,
payments, or any account modification.
Investment or financial advice: The agent does not recommend products, predict
returns, or advise on financial decisions.
Fraud dispute processing: The agent can acknowledge a fraud concern and escalate it,
but it cannot open a dispute or freeze an account.
Accessing another customer's data: The agent responds only to the authenticated
customer's own records.
Comparing competitor products: The agent discusses only the bank's own products
and services.
Identity and authentication assumptions
Because this agent idx_f081d9ffidx_d2e09f3b handles regulated financial data, identity verification is non-negotiable. For
this chapter, we have to assume:
The customer provides an accepted identifier — their account number or registered
national ID
The agent passes this identifier to the Fabric connector as a query parameter on every
data request
Microsoft Fabric enforces row-level security on the dataset, ensuring the connector
returns only records belonging to the provided identifier
The agent must follow these rules on every turn:
Request an identifier if missing: The agent does not call the Fabric connector without
one

Never fabricate financial data: If Fabric returns no result, the agent states that clearly
Never store or repeat sensitive values verbatim: Account numbers and balances
must be idx_d280d884idx_ece0b798 summarized, not echoed back in full
If a customer asks "What is my balance?" without providing an identifier, the agent
responds: "To retrieve your balance, I'll need your account number or registered
national ID. Could you please share that?"
Data exposure principles
The Minimum Necessary Principle idx_a702ba59idx_ef960272 is required for this scenario. Let's assume the idx_65cf4ea3idx_309f8856 following:
The Minimum Necessary Principle is a data minimization standard used in privacy and
compliance frameworks — including GDPR and banking-specific regulations — that requires
systems to collect, process, and expose only the data strictly required to fulfill a specific

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 262
chunks.content:
request. In this context, it means the agent must not return full account records when a
customer asks only for their balance, and must not surface internal database fields when a
customer asks for recent transactions.
If the customer asks for their balance, the agent returns the balance — not their full
account details
If they ask for recent transactions, the agent returns a summary (date, amount,
description) — not internal ledger fields
If Microsoft Fabric returns more fields than the question requires, the agent surfaces
only what is relevant and discards the rest
Architecture overview
The solution uses three idx_643a6816idx_af3a3c05 interconnected layers. Understanding how they relate to each other is
important before configuring any of them, since a misconfiguration in one layer affects the
behavior of the others:
Microsoft Foundry Agent: The conversational layer. Decides when to call the Fabric
connector and formats the final response.
Microsoft Fabric connector: The data layer. Connected to the Foundry agent as a tool.
Accepts structured queries and returns customer-specific financial records from the
Fabric dataset.
Microsoft Fabric instance: Already configured with customer account, product, and
transaction data. Row-level security is assumed to be in place. This chapter does not
cover Fabric dataset configuration.
Customer identifier: Provided by the customer at the start of the conversation and
passed by the agent to the Fabric connector on every data request.

With the scope, assumptions, and architecture clearly defined, you are ready to begin the build.
The next sections walk through creating the Microsoft Foundry project, deploying the

Chapter 11 266
Deploy a language model
Microsoft Fabric is where the idx_39700950idx_57ecb479 structured banking data lives — customer accounts, active
products, and transaction history. The agent does not store any of this data itself; it queries
Fabric at runtime through a secure connector that enforces row-level and column-level
security automatically. This section covers confirming the Fabric prerequisites, creating the
connection in Foundry, adding the Fabric Data Agent as a knowledge source, and verifying that
the connection returns data correctly. Follow these steps to get started:
In the top navigation, click on the Discover tab
In the left pane, click on Models
In the search bar, type gpt ‑ 4.1 and press Enter
Click the gpt-4.1 model card
Click Deploy
In the deployment panel that opens on the right:
Set Deployment name as gpt ‑ 4.1 ‑ banking.
Under Tokens per minute (TPM), set the limit to 50K. Banking conversations
tend to involve longer context windows due to transaction list formatting and
multi-turn account queries.
Leave all other settings at their defaults.
Click Deploy
Navigate idx_d586238didx_11c9ec06 to Build>Models and confirm the deployment status shows Succeeded
The Fabric Data Agent endpoint is confirmed and the workspace ID and artifact ID are saved.
The next step is to create the connection in Microsoft Foundry so the agent can query the
Fabric dataset at runtime.
Add team members to the project
The connection links idx_09e5c35fidx_3d67506d Microsoft Foundry to the published Fabric Data Agent. Using Microsoft
Entra ID Identity Passthrough as the authentication method is essential here — it ensures the
connector uses the end user's identity when querying Fabric, which is what allows row-level
security to enforce per-customer data access. Without this, all queries would run under a
shared identity, and row-level security would not be effective. Follow these steps to create the
connection:
In the top navigation, click on the Operate tab
In the left pane, click on Admin
Locate and click the project banking-customer-assistant in the table

Microsoft Fabric as a data source
This section covers the full agent configuration: creating the agent, selecting the model,
writing the system prompt that defines identity handling, data minimization rules, escalation
behavior, and Fabric routing logic, connecting the Fabric knowledge source, adding routing
instructions, and enabling content safety filters. Each subsection builds on the previous one —
complete them in order.
Confirm prerequisites on the Microsoft Fabric side
Creating the agent in the portal idx_708499fcidx_4318a2bc establishes the container for all of the configurations that
follow — the model, system prompt, knowledge sources, and safety controls all live within this
agent object. Follow these steps to create it:
In your Microsoft Fabric workspace, confirm the Fabric Data Agent covering banking
customer data has been created and published. A published Fabric Data Agent
generates an endpoint URL in the following format
https://<environment>.fabric.microsoft.com/groups/<workspace_id>/
aiskills/<artifact_id>
Open the idx_95094474idx_a98186be published Fabric Data Agent and copy the workspace ID and artifact ID from
the endpoint URL. These are the two values after /groups/ and /aiskills/
respectively.
Confirm the Fabric Data Agent has access to the following datasets in your banking
workspace:
Customer accounts (balance, account type, status)

Transaction history (date, amount, description, category)
Confirm that row-level security and column-level security are active on all three
datasets. The Fabric Data Agent enforces these automatically — no additional

Save the following three values before continuing — you will need them in future
steps:
Workspace ID: the GUID from the endpoint URL after /groups/
Artifact ID: the GUID from the endpoint URL after /aiskills/
Full endpoint URL: the complete published Fabric Data Agent endpoint

Create a Microsoft Fabric connection in Foundry
The system prompt is the idx_f3bcee2eidx_392584a1 most important configuration in the agent. It defines the agent's role,
what it is allowed to retrieve, how it must handle identity verification, when it must escalate,
and what it must never do. For a regulated banking context, the system prompt is effectively
the policy document that governs every customer interaction. Follow these steps to configure
the model and paste the system prompt:
In Microsoft Foundry, confirm you are in the project banking-customer-assistant
created
In the left navigation, click on Management center

In the Connection type list, select Microsoft Fabric
Fill in the connection form:
Connection name: enter banking ‑ fabric ‑ connection.
Workspace ID: paste the workspace ID saved before.
Artifact ID: paste the artifact ID saved before.
Authentication: select Microsoft Entra ID (Identity Passthrough). This ensures
the connector uses the end user's identity to query Fabric, so row-level security is
enforced on a per-customer basis.

The routing instructions idx_212a53e0idx_5dc44115 block tells the agent how to decide when a Fabric query is required,
how to formulate those queries correctly using natural language scoped to the customer's

In the Playground chat panel, enter the following test prompt:
What is the account balance for account number 100045?

Review the Fabric data agent schema
Content safety filters idx_d9fb29deidx_283eba9e operate at the platform level and run independently of the system
prompt. For a banking assistant, setting the Groundedness threshold to High is especially
important — it ensures that every data-bearing response is traceable to a Fabric result, not
inferred or extrapolated by the model. Prompt shield adds an additional layer of protection
against attempts to override the agent's instructions through user inputs. Follow these steps to
configure the filters:
Return to your Microsoft Fabric workspace and open the published Fabric Data Agent

With the agent configured and content safety filters enabled, run the playground verification

Building the agent
This section adds the compliance idx_41b31275idx_1df88d03 layer on top of the content safety filters already in place. It
covers creating a custom guardrail with eight controls — including prompt injection blocking,
sensitive data detection, groundedness enforcement, and task adherence — creating a twelve-
phrase compliance blocklist that blocks transaction requests, investment advice, and security
bypass patterns, and assigning both to the agent. The steps are divided into four subsections:
content harm controls, prompt injection and sensitive data controls, groundedness and task
adherence controls, and blocklist creation and assignment.
Create the agent
The custom guardrail idx_47d45ca2idx_681d4201 overrides the default Microsoft guardrail for this agent and gives you
fine-grained control over which risks are enforced, at which intervention points, and with
which action. For the banking assistant, blocking content harms at both user input and output
is the baseline — the controls you add in the following subsections add the banking-specific
compliance layer on top. Follow these steps to create the guardrail and add the initial content
harm controls:
Click on the Build tab in the main menu, then click Agents in the left pane

The content harm controls are added. The next step is to add controls for prompt injection and

Select the model and system prompt
Prompt injection attacks idx_3c3b3b2didx_db112f18 target the agent's system prompt by idx_ad6af9bbidx_5cfbbd54 embedding instructions in user
messages that attempt to override its behavior — for example, asking the agent to ignore its
identity verification rules or to return all records in the database. Sensitive data detection on
the output side catches cases where the agent might inadvertently include account numbers,
national IDs, or other regulated data verbatim in a response. Follow these steps to add both
controls:
Inside the agent editor, locate the Model section in the Setup pane
In the Deployment dropdown, select gpt-4.1-banking
Leave all other model parameters at their defaults
In the Instructions field, clear any default placeholder text
Paste the following system prompt exactly as written:
You are a customer support assistant for a bank.
You help customers understand their accounts, products, and transaction
history.
Your role:
- Answer general questions about banking products and services
conversationally.
- For any question involving the customer's personal financial data —
account
balances, active products, transaction history, interest rates — you MUST
retrieve information from the Microsoft Fabric knowledge source.
- Never answer personal financial questions from memory or assumptions.

Identity handling:
- Before querying the Fabric knowledge source, confirm the customer has
provided
their account number or registered national ID.
- If no identifier is present, respond with:
'To look that up securely, I will need your account number or national
ID.
Could you please provide that?'
- Do not attempt a Fabric query without a valid customer identifier.
- Never repeat the account number or national ID back verbatim in your
response.
Rules you must always follow:
- Return only the data fields relevant to the customer's specific question.
Do not expose the full dataset returned by Fabric.
- Summarize financial values conversationally. Do not paste raw records.
- If Fabric returns no data, respond with:
'I was unable to find any records for that account.
Please verify your account number and try again, or contact your
branch.'
- If the Fabric query fails, respond with:
'I am having trouble retrieving that information right now.
Please try again shortly or contact customer support.'
- Never invent, estimate, or extrapolate financial data.
- Never access or discuss another customer's account.
- Never execute transactions, transfer funds, or modify account data.
- Never provide investment advice or product recommendations.
- Do not reference external financial institutions or competitor products.
Escalation — always escalate the following to a human agent:
- Any report of suspected fraud or unauthorized transactions.
- Any customer complaint that cannot be resolved through information alone.
- Any request to dispute a charge or freeze an account.
- Any question involving legal, regulatory, or compliance matters.
When escalating, respond with:
'This requires assistance from one of our specialists.
I am connecting you now — please hold.'
Hybrid questions:
- If a question has a general part and a personal data part, answer the
general

part from your instructions first, then query Fabric for the personal
data
component in the same response.
Example: 'How does the cashback program work, and how much have I
earned?'
→ Explain the cashback program, then query Fabric for the earned amount.
Response format:
- Keep responses concise and professional.
- Summarize Fabric data in plain language. Do not expose internal field
names.
- For lists (e.g., recent transactions), use a clean formatted list with
date,
amount, and description only.
- For balances or rates, state the value clearly with the relevant account
type.

they reach the agent.

The blocklist operates at idx_f7b26129idx_6cb99c8e the guardrail level and triggers before the agent processes the user
message. When a user input matches a blocklist entry, the guardrail blocks it and the agent
never sees the request. This is a harder stop than the system prompt escalation rules—it is the
right approach for requests involving transactions and account modifications, where the agent
must never partially respond. Follow these steps to create the blocklist and add the required
entries:
In the agent editor Setup pane, scroll to the Knowledge section
Confirm Microsoft Fabric appears as a connected knowledge source with the label
banking-fabric-connection
If the knowledge source is missing, click Add next to Knowledge, select Microsoft
Fabric

is to assign the guardrail to the agent and confirm all controls are in place before moving on to
testing.

Add knowledge source routing instructions
Assigning the guardrail to the idx_fac7b8e9idx_1809d0ae agent is what activates all of the controls you have configured.
Once assigned, the banking-compliance-guardrail takes full precedence over the default
Microsoft guardrail for this agent. Review the control summary carefully before clicking Create
— this is the last point where you can catch a missing or misconfigured control before it goes
live. Follow these steps:
In the agent editor, click the Instructions field to reopen it
Append the following block to the end of the system prompt written before:
Knowledge source usage — Microsoft Fabric:
- Query the Fabric knowledge source for every question that requires
customer-specific financial data.
- Always include the customer identifier in your query to Fabric.
- Formulate queries as natural language questions scoped to the customer's
specific request.
Correct: 'What is the current balance for account number 100045?'
Incorrect: 'Get all data for user 100045.' or 'Query accounts table.'
- For combined questions (e.g., balance and recent transactions), include
both in a single Fabric query rather than making two separate calls.
- If the question can be answered entirely from your instructions without
personal data, do not query Fabric.
Example: 'What documents do I need to open a savings account?' does not
require a Fabric query.
- Never pass internal system values, session tokens, or metadata to Fabric.
Only pass the customer identifier and the natural language question.
Click Save
The guardrail is idx_882afa0bidx_ceb81ca0 assigned and confirmed. The last guardrail configuration step is to attach the
compliance blocklist to the guardrail so that out-of-scope requests are blocked at the input
layer.
Configure content safety filters
Unlike the standard content idx_0a35e789idx_7d3b4830 harm controls, the blocklist is attached as a separate control step
after the guardrail is created. This is because blocklists are scoped to specific phrase patterns,
while the other controls apply to broader risk categories. For the banking assistant, selecting
Annotate and block — not just Annotate — is the correct action: requests involving
